title: H. G. Wells: The War of the Worlds — Ep 25/27 — "The Dead London"
description:
He stumbles past the bridge where a dust-blackened man swings at his head, too drunk to speak; he steadies him and walks on. The road east thickens with black dust and the dead lie softened along it. Gold chains lie untouched on a doorstep where a woman sleeps dead, and a white terrace burns at the road's end, its roar almost a mercy.

Near South Kensington a two-note howl rises from the empty houses, and he finds a fighting-machine standing over the park. He sleeps in a public house, wakes at dusk, and goes on past a wrecked machine toward a second one, a starving dog and its pack racing past him with red meat in its jaws. On the canal bridge the cry stops dead, and the silence hits him like thunder: "It has stopped. God help me, it has stopped."

He hides in a cabmen's shelter past midnight. Before dawn a third machine stands on Primrose Hill, and he means to die there until he sees birds tearing at brown shreds on its hood, and runs instead, wading breast-high through the flood and up the rampart in a wild, trembling joy.

Below him the pit holds the fallen machines, and the Martians lie dead, killed where men failed by Earth's smallest things, its germs. "Dead! They are dead, every one of them!" he cries, and the sunrise sets the dead engines glittering as he gives thanks aloud, hands raised, before the thought of his wife and the old life gone for ever brings his hands down and his shoulders shaking.

Chapter VIII of Book Two of H. G. Wells's The War of the Worlds (1898), "Dead London", in the public domain.

— The Keeper's Lantern —
Every episode is one whole chapter, in order, from the first page to the last.
